title: Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE
Github : Lab 4
What happens when an LLM inference service receives:

longer prompts
repeated context
longer outputs
more concurrent users

Do all of these workloads affect the system in the same way? And when performance starts degrading, should we simply add another replica based on CPU utilization? That is what I wanted to understand in Lab 4. In the previous lab, I deployed LLM-D with a CPU-based vLLM model server on an existing Oracle Kubernetes Engine cluster. Lab 4 extends that setup with:

Prometheus
Grafana
KEDA
LLM-D demand metrics
OKE Cluster Autoscaler
repeatable workload experiments
The goal was not only to autoscale the deployment. The bigger goal was to make the inference system observable enough to understand why it should scale.
What was the main question behind this lab?
The main question was:

Can we scale an inference service
based on actual inference demand
instead of only infrastructure utilization?
Traditional application autoscaling often starts with CPU utilization. For example:

CPU above 70%
→ add another pod
That can be useful, but LLM inference has more direct signals:

How many requests are running?
How many requests are waiting?
Is TTFT increasing?
Is KV cache being reused?
Are model servers running out of capacity?

A model server may already have high active concurrency or user-visible queueing before an average CPU metric tells a useful story. So this lab intentionally used LLM-D EPP demand metrics as the primary autoscaling signals. The simplified architecture was:

Client / Benchmark Workload
        ↓
LLM-D EPP / Routing Layer
        ↓
CPU vLLM Model-Server Pods
        ↓
Prometheus collects metrics
        ↓
Grafana shows system behavior
        ↓
KEDA queries Prometheus
        ↓
Generated HPA scales model pods
        ↓
If a new pod cannot fit:
OKE Cluster Autoscaler adds a node
The important point is that this contains two different scaling layers.

KEDA
=
scales model-server pods

OKE Cluster Autoscaler
=
adds cluster nodes

KEDA can request another vLLM replica, but it cannot create CPU or memory capacity. OKE Cluster Autoscaler only becomes involved when Kubernetes has created a pod that cannot be scheduled on the existing nodes.
What observability stack did I use?
The lab installed a dedicated monitoring stack containing:

Prometheus through kube-prometheus-stack
Grafana
KEDA
ServiceMonitor-based metric discovery
LLM-D Grafana dashboards: Grafana remained internal to the cluster. Instead of exposing it through a public ingress, the workbench opened a local kubectl port-forward connection:

kubectl --context <context> -n llm-d-monitoring \
  port-forward service/llmd-grafana 3000:80
This made the dashboards available on:

The lab intentionally kept Grafana private and accessed it only through the local tunnel. which metrics did I watch? One of the biggest lessons was that inference performance cannot be understood through one metric. I watched:

Time to First Token
Inter-token latency
End-to-end request latency
Requests per second
Generated tokens per second
Prompt-token throughput
KV-cache hit rate
KV-cache usage
Active requests
Waiting requests
EPP queue depth
Ready and Pending replicas
Node count
Each metric describes a different part of the request lifecycle.

TTFT
=
How long before generation begins?

Inter-token latency
=
How quickly tokens continue after the first token?

End-to-end latency
=
How long does the full request occupy the system?

KV-cache hit rate
=
How much prompt processing is being reused?

Queue depth
=
How much work cannot currently enter a backend?

Running requests
=
How much active serving demand exists?
Looking at only one of them can lead to the wrong conclusion.
How did I keep the experiments meaningful?
The lab used five repeatable workload recipes. The important rule was:
Change one workload characteristic at a time.
Before the cache experiments, I restarted the model-server deployment to clear the in-memory prefix cache and reset cumulative counters. I then ran:

1. Short unique prompts
2. Long unique prompts
3. Long shared-prefix prompts
4. Long outputs
5. Sustained concurrent traffic
This made it easier to connect each workload change with the dashboard behavior.
Experiment 1 — What happens with short, unique prompts?
The first experiment established the baseline. It used:

100 short prompts
concurrency 1
maximum output 128 tokens
no intentional shared prefix
The approximate endpoint-level results were:

Generated throughput: 41.5 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 144 ms
Approximate ITL: 34 ms
The dashboards showed:

low TTFT
stable inter-token latency
almost no queueing
near-zero prefix-cache hit rate
little persistent KV-cache use after completion This became the control case. Short unique prompts require relatively little prefill work and provide almost nothing for prefix caching to reuse.
Experiment 2 — What changes with long, unique prompts?
The second experiment increased prompt length but intentionally kept every prompt unique. The approximate results were:

Generated throughput: 32.4 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 764 ms
Approximate ITL: 36 ms
TTFT increased dramatically:
But inter-token latency stayed close to the baseline:

34 ms
→
36 ms

This made the prefill/decode distinction visible. The model had much more prompt context to process before producing the first token. That increased TTFT. But once decoding started, the cadence between generated tokens remained comparatively stable. The lesson was:

Long input
primarily stresses prefill.
Experiment 3 — What changes when the long prefix is reused?
The third experiment used long prompts again, but this time every prompt shared the same large initial prefix. Only the final suffix changed. The approximate results were:

KV-cache hit rate: 53%
Generated throughput: 39.9 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 172 ms
Approximate ITL: 36.5 ms
Compare the two long-prompt workloads:

Cold long unique:
p95 TTFT ≈ 764 ms

Warm shared prefix:
p95 TTFT ≈ 172 ms

The prompt was still long. But the model no longer needed to repeat all of the prefill computation. The shared KV state could be reused. Inter-token latency remained broadly stable because prefix caching mainly improves:

prompt processing
and
time to first token
It does not create the same dramatic improvement in decode speed. This is why prefix caching can be useful for:

repeated system prompts
policy instructions
RAG instruction blocks
long shared documents
multi-turn conversation history The first uncached request could still appear in p99 TTFT, but once the cache warmed, the following requests became much faster.
Experiment 4 — What happens when outputs become much longer?
The fourth experiment kept concurrency at one but increased the maximum output to approximately 512 tokens. The approximate results were:

50 successful requests
Generated throughput: 41.7 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 146 ms
Approximate ITL: 35.6 ms
p95 end-to-end latency: 16 seconds

TTFT and inter-token latency remained close to the original baseline. But the complete request took much longer. Why? Because each request occupied the model server for many more decode iterations. The model was not necessarily generating each token more slowly. It was simply generating many more tokens. The lesson was:

Long output
=
more decode work
+
longer request residence time
This reduces completed requests per second and increases the chance of contention when multiple users arrive.
Experiment 5 — What changes when concurrency increases?
The final experiment used sustained mixed traffic with:

concurrency 8
maximum output 128 tokens
At the captured moment, Grafana showed:

Running requests: 8
Waiting requests: 0

TTFT p50: approximately 112 ms
TTFT p95: approximately 236 ms
TTFT p99: approximately 247 ms

ITL p50: approximately 38 ms
ITL p95: approximately 50 ms

Request throughput: approximately 0.74 requests/sec
KV-cache hit rate: approximately 52%
Even without a persistently non-zero queue, the active-request count was high enough to request more capacity. This was an important observation:
Queue depth is not the only demand signal.
Eight active requests already represented enough concurrent work for KEDA to scale the deployment.
Which autoscaling metrics did KEDA use?
The KEDA policy used two LLM-D EPP metrics:

llm_d_epp_flow_control_queue_size

llm_d_epp_request_running
The first measured requests waiting because backend capacity was unavailable. The second measured active in-flight requests. The default policy was:

Minimum replicas: 1
Maximum replicas: 3
Queue threshold: 1 per replica
Running-request threshold: 4 per replica
Polling interval: 15 seconds
Scale-down stabilization: 5 minutes
KEDA evaluated both signals and used the larger desired replica calculation. The active-request calculation was:

Active requests = 8

Threshold
= 4 requests per replica

Desired replicas
= ceil(8 / 4)
= 2

KEDA’s generated HPA therefore requested a second CPU vLLM pod. This was the pod-scaling event. But the cluster did not have enough available CPU and memory to schedule that pod. So the second replica stayed:
Pending
That Pending pod was not a failed autoscaling result. It was the next signal in the scaling chain.
How did node scaling happen?
Once the pod was Pending because its resource requests could not fit, OKE Cluster Autoscaler had a legitimate reason to add capacity. The full sequence was:

1. Concurrent traffic increases.

2. LLM-D reports active requests
   and/or queue depth.

3. Prometheus stores the metrics.

4. KEDA queries Prometheus.

5. The generated HPA requests
   another vLLM pod.

6. Kubernetes creates the pod.

7. The pod cannot fit
   and remains Pending.

8. OKE Cluster Autoscaler
   adds a managed node.

9. The pod moves:
   Pending
   → ContainerCreating
   → Running
   → Ready
This distinction is important:

KEDA responds to inference demand.

OKE Cluster Autoscaler responds
to unschedulable Kubernetes capacity demand.

They solve two related but different problems. Why not scale nodes immediately? Because additional pods may already fit on existing nodes. If every pod scale-out directly created a new node, the cluster could add unnecessary infrastructure. Kubernetes first tries to place the new replica using available capacity. Only when the requested CPU and memory cannot fit does node autoscaling become necessary. So the correct sequence is:

Demand
→ Pod
→ Scheduling decision
→ Node, only when needed
Why did the endpoint and Grafana show different values?

Another useful lesson was that the workbench and Grafana did not always report identical latency numbers. The workbench measured requests at the local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. That measurement included:

router overhead
network overhead
streaming behavior
client-side timing
The vLLM Grafana metrics were emitted closer to the model server. So both measurements were valid, but they represented different parts of the request path. The lesson was:

Before comparing two metrics,
understand where each one is measured.
The same name does not always mean the same measurement boundary. What did this lab teach me? The first lesson was:

TTFT and inter-token latency
tell different stories.
Long prompts increased TTFT because they increased prefill work. They did not create the same increase in inter-token latency. The second lesson was:
Prefix caching primarily improves prefill.
The warm shared-prefix workload reduced TTFT significantly, while decode cadence remained relatively stable. The third lesson was:
Output length is an occupancy problem.
Long outputs keep requests inside the model server for longer, even when tokens continue arriving at a stable rate. The fourth lesson was:

Concurrency connects benchmarking
to autoscaling.
A system that looks healthy at concurrency one may behave very differently when eight requests are active. The fifth lesson was:

Autoscaling should use signals
that represent actual inference demand.
CPU utilization remains useful for diagnosis, but active requests and queue depth are closer to the user-facing serving problem. And finally:

Pod scaling and node scaling
must be understood as one chain.
A model-serving platform is not fully elastic if it can request a pod but cannot create the infrastructure required to run it.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Before this lab, it was easy to think about autoscaling as:

Load increases
→ Add more servers
The real system is more layered:

Workload shape
changes inference behavior.

Inference behavior
changes TTFT, ITL, cache usage,
queueing, and active concurrency.

Inference metrics
drive pod scaling.

Unschedulable pods
drive infrastructure scaling.
So autoscaling is not a separate infrastructure feature sitting outside inference. It is connected directly to:

prefill
decode
KV-cache reuse
request residence time
concurrency
routing
capacity
What is the key intuition?
The simplest summary is:

Prompt length changes prefill.

Shared context changes cache economics.

Output length changes decode occupancy.

Concurrency changes the scaling story.
Lab 4 made these relationships visible on a real Kubernetes deployment. It also showed how:

LLM-D
+
vLLM
+
Prometheus
+
Grafana
+
KEDA
+
OKE Cluster Autoscaler
can work together as one observable and demand-driven inference platform.
What comes next?
Now that the scaling sequence is visible, the next question becomes:

How do we turn these experiments
into an actual capacity plan?
That means connecting:

prompt distribution
output distribution
concurrency
TTFT targets
replica count
node size
scale-up time
cost
Because autoscaling can react to demand. But good capacity planning decides how much warm capacity should already exist before that demand arrives.
